etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: いかに (ikani) + も (mo)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Uncertain. Perhaps from archaic おおけなし (ookenashi, “impudent, undisciplined”). Alternately, perhaps from おっかながる (okkanagaru, “to be afraid, be nervous”). The Linguistic Atlas of Japan suggested that the word was once common in the Tōhoku and Kantō regions, but it became increasingly colloquial or intimate during the early modern period (c. 17th to 19th century).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Sound shift from 取(と)りて (torite).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English dump.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English battery

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English pot.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Sinitic 中斷 /中断 (zhōngduàn).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of し (shi, “doing”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb する suru “to do”) + 上げる (ageru, “to raise up; to bring to an end”). Derived via regular historical processes from older 仕上ぐ (shiagu), a 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verb.
Compare the English expression to do something up → to do something thoroughly.
The 仕 kanji for the first character is an example of phonetic ateji.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 値(ね) (ne, “price; cost”) + 打(う)ち (uchi)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 共(とも) (tomo-) + 働(はたら)き (hataraki, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 働(はたら)く (hataraku).). The hataraki changes to bataraki as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 嘆く (nage₂ku, “to sigh; to grieve over; to lament”). In turn, verbalized from noun 嘆き (nage₂ki₁, “sigh; lament”), derived as a compound of 長 (naga, “long”) + 息 (iki₁, “breath”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 器 (khijᴴ, “vessel; instrument”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ut͡supa/ → /ut͡suɸa/ → /ut͡suwa/
From Old Japanese. Cognate with 空 (utsuo, ancient utsupo, utsubo), signifying a hollowness. Appears to be a compound of 空, 内 (utsu, “hollow”, combining form, standalone form uchi, “inside”) + は (ha). The derivation of this ha element is unclear.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Adjectivization of verb 好(この)む (konomu, “to prefer, to like”), using the adjectivizing suffix しい (-shii, “that kind of thing, that kind of quality”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 対 (tai, “place in opposition and compare”) + 比 (hi, “compare”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/neu/ → /njoː/
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 尿 (MC newH, “urine”).
First attested in 1275.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 湯(ゆ) (yu, “warm water”) + 放(ま)り (mari, “excretion”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 放(ま)る (maru, “to excrete”)).
First cited to the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/jumari/ → /jubari/
From 尿(ゆまり) (yumari). Bilabial nasal /m/ loses nasality, becoming /b/. Likely due to lexicalization of the term, and a loss of awareness of the origins of the mari portion.
First cited to the Wamyō Ruijushō of roughly 934 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/jumari/ → /jubari/ → */jʉbari/ → /ibari/
Shift from 尿(ゆばり) (yubari).
First attested in c. 950 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shortening of 尿(ゆばり) (yubari) or 尿(いばり) (ibari).
First attested in the early 1300s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Unknown. Possibly onomatopoeia.
First cited to the Utsubo Monogatari of roughly 999 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From baby talk, as a reduplication of the initial shi- in 尿(しと) (shito).
First cited to a text from the late Muromachi period (late 1500s).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɕito/ → /ɕi/ → /ɕiː/
From baby talk. From 尿(しと) (shito), formed by dropping the second syllable and lengthening the vowel.
/ɕiɕi/ → /ɕiːɕiː/ → /ɕiː/
Alternatively, from 尿(しし) (shishi), formed by lengthening the vowel and dropping the second syllable.
First attested in the late 1700s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 帯ぶ (obu), then following 四段活用 (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade conjugation”). Later on, it shifted to 上二段活用 (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”), the precursor to the modern 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨sipu⟩ → ⟨sipuru⟩ → /ɕiɸuɾu/ → /ɕiɸɨɾu/ → /ɕiwiɾu/ → /ɕiiɾu/
From Old Japanese 強ふ (sipu), in the 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.
Related to 誣(し)いる (shiiru, “to slander; to defame”). Possibly related to 癈いる (shiiru, “to lose function (said of body organs)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 心(しん) (shin, “heart, mind, spirit”) + 中(ちゅう) (-chū, “center, throughout”, rendaku form 中(じゅう) (jū)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 心中 (MC sim trjuwng, literally “heart + center, middle, within”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kokoro moti/ → /kokorʉmʉti/ → */kokomʉti/ → /kokot͡ɕi/
Sound shift from 心持ち (kokoromochi, “nature; feeling, mood”).
The kanji spelling is ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), borrowed from Chinese 心地 (xīndì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/siːm diː/ → /simdi/ → /ɕimd͡ʑi/ → /ɕiɲd͡ʑi/
From Middle Chinese 心地 (MC sim dijH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of さ (sa) + 擦る (suru, “to rub”). The sa element is unclear.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of 果てる (hateru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: A surface analysis suggests a compound of the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of classical Japanese verb 潤(うる)ふ (urufu) + ふ (fu, auxiliary verb expressing repetition or ongoing state). Related to 閏(うるう) (urū).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 肝(かん) (kan, “liver”) + 腎(じん) (jin, “kidney”). 心 is a daiyōji replacing 腎; the じん (jin) reading of 心 is not an example of rendaku.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. One of the oldest attested words in the Japanese language, used in the Man'yōshū and Nihon Shoki.
This character usually means a type of fungus in Chinese. However, it was also used phonetically in 芝麻 (*chimæ, “sesame”) (modern Mandarin 芝麻 (zhīmá)), and it seems that the Japanese use of this character for the sense of grass may have come from this sesame sense in Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of し (shi, adjectival ending) + 様 (sama, “kind, type”). The sama changes to zama as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The kanji 芝 was used as an ateji, probably based on its on'yomi of shi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 芝 (*chi). Compare modern Mandarin 芝 (zhī).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Used as ateji in various surnames.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
見(み) (mi, “looking”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)る (miru, “to see, look”)) + 苦(くる)しい (kurushii, “painful, agonising”).
The kurushii changes to gurushii as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 趣(おもむ)く (omomuku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *arare.
Attested from the 8th century. From Proto-Japonic *arare. In Man'yōshū (a. 759) 霰(あられ) (arare) appears to refer either to small bits of hail or graupel, or to larger hailstones (contemporary 雹(ひょう) (hyō)).
Compare dialectal 霰 (arane), Miyako 霰 (arari), Yaeyama 霰 (arari).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle Chinese 飽和
